analysis.one_liner: Taxes away all oil profits above $75 a barrel and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on May 13, 2026 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has received no further action and attracted no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a windfall tax on companies that produce or import more than 100,000 barrels of crude oil a day during what it calls the Iran War oil crisis. The tax equals 100 percent of everything a barrel sells for above $75 (adjusted for inflation). All money collected would go into a relief fund and be paid out as refundable tax credits — gasoline price rebates — to individual taxpayers. The tax and the rebates would continue until the President declares hostilities with Iran have ended, the Strait of Hormuz is fully reopened, and oil falls below $75 a barrel.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual taxpayers, who would receive quarterly refundable credits funded by the oil tax, with an outreach program so people know they are eligible. Residents of U.S. territories would get equivalent payments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyday taxpayers facing high gas prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an excise tax on each barrel of taxable crude oil (including gasoline and diesel) extracted in or imported to the U.S. by companies producing or importing more than 100,000 barrels a day, at a rate equal to 100 percent of the price of oil above $75 per barrel (inflation-adjusted after 2026).

All revenue goes into an Iran War Gasoline Price Relief Fund and is paid out to eligible individuals as a refundable quarterly credit against income tax, with Treasury required to run an outreach program so taxpayers know how to claim it.

The tax and rebates stay in effect until the President declares hostilities with Iran have ceased, the Strait of Hormuz is fully reopened, and oil prices fall below $75 a barrel, tying relief directly to the crisis conditions.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil producers and importers — companies averaging more than 100,000 barrels a day — which would surrender all revenue per barrel above the $75 threshold. To the extent they pass costs through, consumers at the pump would bear part of it.

drawbacks.text: A 100 percent rate on every dollar of price above $75 gives companies no reward for producing an extra barrel during a shortage, a design economists warn can discourage the additional drilling and imports that would actually bring prices down.
The tax applies to gasoline and diesel as well as crude, so if oil companies pass the excise through to prices, the pump savings the rebate is meant to deliver could be partly offset.
The rebate amount each quarter is simply 'determined by the Secretary' based on revenue collected, leaving the size and timing of household payments vague and dependent on administrative discretion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the crisis it targets were real, the rebate would put money directly in households' pockets and claw back wartime oil profits, a strong deal for ordinary people. The main honest objection is design: a full 100 percent tax above the threshold is blunt and could discourage the extra supply that lowers prices, and some of the tax could leak into pump prices before the rebate ever arrives. As written, the benefit to households outweighs the drawbacks, but the bill is a statement rather than a negotiated compromise.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on May 13, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No further action appears in the record: the committee has not scheduled a hearing or a vote, and no member of either party has signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil companies, which face no tax while the bill sits untouched, and the Ways and Means Committee's leadership, which has avoided a vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies, since no tax was enacted

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the windfall profits tax and rebate bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (chair)
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since referral — no markup, hearing, or floor scheduling — leaving it unvoted.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill has a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so its support has never been tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Large crude oil producers and importers
industries.note: Companies averaging over 100,000 barrels a day would pay 100 percent of everything above $75 per barrel on both domestic extraction and imports, including gasoline and diesel. That surrender of wartime windfall profits is the money funding the household rebates.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since its May referral, the bill is on the standard path of a single-member messaging bill: it will almost certainly die at the end of the 119th Congress without a hearing or a vote.
